 GLEN CANYON RECREATION AREA, Utah (KUTV) — The Glen Canyon Institute calls the recent rise in Lake Powell’s water level an “opportunity” to consider bolder, larger solutions to stabilize the water supply and dam operations.
 Recent storms raised the reservoir’s level by more than 20 feet, adding about 1.2 million acre-feet of water, according to Utah State University. But the reservoir is still about one-quarter full.
 “This boost might give the Upper Basin states a couple more years before they really need to be worrying to the same extent as we were starting to worry before we got these big storms,” said Gina Gilson, interim director of the USU Center for Colorado River Studies.

 Gilson said the increased water level is a short-term boost.
 “We have a lot bigger problem than just how much water is in a reservoir in a given year. It's a bigger systemic challenge that needs to be addressed,” Gilson said.
 The Glen Canyon Institute calls the added water supply a cushion that provides time to consider long-term plans, such as “Fill Mead First.”
 “None of the big-picture problems have been solved, and so we're going to keep doing what we have always been doing, which is supporting science and research and using that to advocate for the restoration of Glen Canyon,” said Zanna Stutz, program director of the Glen Canyon Institute.
 The nation’s two largest reservoirs, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, are each about one-quarter full. Both face threats to their ability to pass water and generate hydropower.
 The “Fill Mead First” proposal suggests allowing water to pass through Lake Powell to fill Lake Mead first, with the goal of ensuring operational success and restoring the surrounding ecosystem. Lake Powell would then be filled if water supplies are high enough.
 Utah State University says the idea is becoming a more legitimate consideration, but it was not included in federal intervention plans this summer.
 “We submitted a bypass alternative to be studied by the Bureau of Reclamation, and the response that we got was that this was an operations EIS, not an infrastructure EIS. So the message we received is that the Bureau wasn't interested in studying an alternative that required infrastructure modifications at Glen Canyon Dam,” Stutz said. “By not studying a bypass alternative, we are just limiting the options and our understanding of said options moving forward. As soon as bypass wasn't going to be studied under that framework, I think it felt challenging to, you know, bring it to the table in other formats, because that's really what the focus was on for Colorado River stakeholders.”
 Stutz said the Bureau of Reclamation needs to consider new operating plans given the low reservoir levels.
 “I think in some ways we are now in a world where we can take a step back and be out of the nitty-gritty of the negotiations and start to think about bigger-picture, more creative solutions in some ways,” Stutz said.
 The Bureau of Reclamation has been conducting a study on Glen Canyon Dam infrastructure modifications for several years, with little public visibility. The agency has held one public webinar on the study.
 The study’s results were not included in the final environmental impact statement the Bureau of Reclamation released earlier this year. The Glen Canyon Institute said they should have been included for the sake of public transparency. The findings are expected by the end of the year.
 Gilson said high-water years like this one could delay or weaken the argument for changes because the reservoirs can currently operate.
 She said proposals will also need to address questions about the feasibility of modifying the infrastructure.
 “It's always refreshing when there's different ideas that are brought to the table for other ways that we could think about operating these reservoirs. But I still think we're a ways off of that becoming any sort of reality,” Gilson said.
